# Finding data

Nobody made GSE60450 for you. Fu and colleagues sorted two kinds of cell out of
mouse mammary glands and sequenced them. They were after the genes that switch
on when a mouse starts producing milk. They published as PubMed 25730472 and
moved on. The data stayed where they left it, and you've been putting your own
questions to it since Chapter 20, none of which were theirs. One of those rows
is `Brca1`, the gene you looked up in Chapter 5, sitting in somebody else's
experiment the whole time and waiting for Chapter 24.

So somebody has probably already run the experiment behind the question you
wrote in Chapter 22. Where is it, and how do you tell whether it's any use to
you?

## Five archives, and which one your question belongs in

Five names cover almost everything a beginner needs. Each one holds a different
kind of thing, and what it holds decides whether your question belongs there.
Read each paragraph for its last sentence.

The Gene Expression Omnibus, GEO, holds processed data that authors deposited
when they published. One submission is a series with an accession like
`GSE60450`, and inside it sits one record per sample. What you download is
usually a table: one row per gene, one column per sample, plus whatever the
submitters wrote about the samples themselves. Your question belongs in GEO if
it compares how much of something there is between groups that somebody else
has already measured.

The Sequence Read Archive, SRA, holds the reads. Those are the sequencer's raw
output, before anybody decided which gene each read came from. Go to SRA when
the counting has to be redone differently, against another genome build or
another annotation. Now the honest part: nothing in this book can process a raw
read. That needs a terminal, an aligner and a reference genome, which is the
corner of the field Chapter 1 said you'd be giving up.
Learn to recognize an `SRR` accession in a methods section anyway, because it
tells you the authors published their raw data and somebody could check them.

Ensembl isn't an experiment archive at all. It's an annotation source: where
genes sit on a genome, and what each stable identifier refers to. There's a
browser on the front of it that draws a stretch of chromosome with its features
lined up underneath. Your question belongs in Ensembl if it's about what sits
at a coordinate rather than about anyone's measurement.

The UCSC Genome Browser is the second annotation source, and it answers the
same kind of question Ensembl does. It draws a genome region as a stack of
tracks, where each track is one kind of evidence laid out on the same
coordinates. Its Table Browser hands you the rows behind a track as a file you
can keep. Come to UCSC when you want to see what else has been measured across
a region you already care about.

Pick one of those two and stay in it. They overlap heavily, so choose on the
thing that will bite you: UCSC writes the first human chromosome as `chr1` and
Ensembl writes it as `1`.

::: {.trap}
Take coordinates from Ensembl, take a track from UCSC, then join the two on
chromosome. Every row misses, because `1` and `chr1` are different strings and
Python is right about that. You get an empty result and no error message. Join
on a second column as well and you get a partial answer that looks reasonable.
:::

The Cancer Genome Atlas, TCGA, is one specific project rather than an archive
of everything. It profiled tumors across many cancer types and recorded
clinical information for every case, with normal tissue from the same patient
for a lot of them. Its data arrives in two tiers, and which tier a file sits in
decides whether you can open it at all. That split gets its own section below,
because it's the one place in this book where a door is genuinely shut to you.

::: {.asof}
Checked on 2 August 2026. All five of these have been redesigned before and
will be again. Three things survive every redesign: a dataset has an accession,
a record lists its samples, and a file has a size printed next to it. Find
those and the layout doesn't matter.
:::

## Reading a record before you trust it

Once you have a candidate accession, four questions decide whether it's usable.
Ask them in this order, because the cheap ones eliminate most candidates before
you've spent anything.

How many samples are there? What are the groups, and how many samples sit in
each? What is the comparison, and against what? And the fourth, which is the
one that takes practice: what did the submitters not write down?

The first two come off the sample table. Here's the one for GSE60450, which
this book ships as `data/GSE60450_samples.csv` with a row per sample.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

samples = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_samples.csv")
print(len(samples), "samples")
print(samples.groupby(["cell_type", "stage"]).size())
```

Twelve samples, six groups, two apiece. You now know something the accession
alone didn't tell you. Every comparison inside this dataset is two against two,
unless you collapse a factor and make it six against six. Chapter 24 does
exactly that, and says what it costs.

::: {.check}
The total prints as 12 and all six group sizes print as 2. A different total
means you loaded a different file. A group size of 1 or 3 means the same thing.
:::

Third question. There's no control arm here, and that isn't a defect. Nothing
was treated, so there's nothing to leave untreated. Virgin is a baseline
because it comes first in time, not because anybody withheld anything. If your
Chapter 22 question contains the word control, swap it for "compared with
what" and answer that instead.

Fourth question, and it's the one that takes practice. Look at what the count
table records about each sample.

```{python}
counts = pd.read_csv("data/GSE60450_counts.tsv.gz", sep="\t", nrows=1)
for name in list(counts.columns)[2:]:
    print(name)
```

Take the first heading apart. The sample is `MCL1-DG`. Then comes
`BC2CTUACXX`, the flowcell the library ran on, and `ACTTGA`, the index barcode
that told the machine this sample from its neighbors. The lane is `L002`. On
the end sits `R1`, a read number, which Illumina writes into every file it
produces. All of that is sequencing logistics, and not one character of it says
basal or luminal, virgin or lactating.

So the count table at the center of this whole project doesn't know what the
experiment was about. The biology sits on GEO instead, on the sample records,
one per sample. Each of those carries a characteristics block: strain,
genotype, sex, tissue, which cell population got sorted out of the gland, and
the developmental stage. Those records run in a different order from the
columns you just printed, and Chapter 24 is where that bites.

Now read the lane out of every heading. Six say `L001` and six say `L002`.
Write down which six you think are the basal samples before you run the next
block, which joins lane to label on sample name rather than on position:

```{python}
lanes = {c.split("_")[0]: c.split("_")[3] for c in counts.columns[2:]}
samples["lane"] = samples["sample"].map(lanes)
print(samples.groupby(["cell_type", "lane"]).size())
```

All six basal samples ran in lane 2, and all six luminal samples ran in lane 1.
The two move together. So a difference you measure between basal and luminal in
this dataset is also a difference between two lanes, and no arithmetic
afterward pulls them apart. Nothing on the GEO record mentions a lane at all.
It survived because somebody left it in a column heading.

This is the normal condition of public data. Submitters record what their
pipeline emitted, and the design lives somewhere a human typed it. Write down
what's missing, every time. This record doesn't say how old the mice were in
weeks, or when any library was prepared. You got the lane back off a column
heading. Those two are gone. A missing field rarely disqualifies a dataset. It
caps what you may claim from that dataset, and you want the cap written down
before you have a result you like.

::: {.trap}
Two GEO series don't have to mean the same thing by the word expression. One
deposits raw counts, the next counts per million, the next FPKM, the next the
log of one of those. Plenty of files never say which. Numbers from two series
will divide, plot and correlate without complaint, and the answer means
nothing. Whole numbers with lots of zeros usually indicate raw counts, and
decimals mean somebody normalized already. Some tools do emit fractional
counts, so treat that as a first read rather than proof.
:::

## What you're allowed to use

GEO and SRA ask you to sign nothing. The data is public, you download it, you
use it, and no login stands between you and any of it. The courtesy, and I'd
treat it as a rule, is to name the accession and the paper in anything you put
your name on. Say plainly that you didn't generate the data. Chapter 26 shows
where that goes in a README.

TCGA splits in two. The open tier holds the summarized results: expression per
gene, copy number, methylation, the somatic mutation calls, and clinical fields
such as stage and survival time. Those mutation files get masked before
release, which means the columns and the variants that could carry germline
information are stripped out first. Anybody can download the open tier today
with no application. The controlled tier holds anything that could identify a
person, which mostly means the raw reads and the germline variants inside them.

Getting into the controlled tier means a data access request through dbGaP. You
submit it from an eRA Commons account, an institutional signing official
co-signs it, and a data access committee at NIH decides. A signing official is
a named person with the authority to bind an organization to an agreement. Both
the account and the signature come from an institution. You don't have one,
this book has no workaround, and I'd rather tell you now than have you spend an
evening on the form. The boundary isn't there to keep you out. A person's
germline variants identify them the way a fingerprint does, and the people who
donated those samples agreed to a specific set of uses.

Here's what gets left out of that warning. The open tier is far more than you
can work through in three hours a week. A question comparing expression between
tumor and matched normal tissue lives entirely inside it, and so does one
comparing clinical groups. You'll run out of evenings long before you run out
of open data.

## What it costs to fetch

Every download in this book prints its size in the sentence that asks you to
start it. Do the same to yourself: write the byte size next to the accession in
your notes before you fetch anything.

GSE60450's count table is 513,592 bytes, compressed. That's the whole
experiment: 27,179 rows of genes by 12 columns of counts, from samples carrying
between 20,015,386 and 24,723,827 counted reads each. A count is a number and a
read is four lines of text, which is the entire reason the table fits in half a
megabyte.

A download written into a Colab notebook lands on Google's machine rather than
yours. If you're paying by the gigabyte, that's the difference between a size
you pay for and one you don't. It doesn't make raw reads usable, because what's
missing there is the software rather than the disk.

## Exercises

::: {.exercise num="23.1" time="60 minutes"}
::: {.goal}
Find three datasets that could address the question you wrote in Chapter 22,
and put each one through the same four questions.
:::
::: {.given}
The Chapter 22 question, in one sentence, naming a comparison and a
measurement. If you can't write that sentence, go back and write it. No amount
of searching repairs an unshaped question.
:::
::: {.produce}
Three accessions. For each one: the number of samples, the group structure
written as groups by samples per group, one thing the metadata doesn't record,
and the size in bytes of the file you'd actually download.
:::
::: {.check}
Every group structure has to come off the record, not off your sense of how the
experiment must have been run. If you can't state it, write "group structure
not stated" beside that accession and keep the accession in your list. That's a
finding about the dataset rather than a failure of yours, and it's your reason
to go looking for a fourth. Then check yourself for the opposite problem: if
all three are the same organism and the same tissue, you searched one phrase
and took the first page of results.
:::

::: {.answerspace lines="12"}
:::
:::

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="Your search returns thousands of series and none of them match your question"}
GEO search runs over free text that submitters wrote, and submitters don't
agree on words. Take the exact phrase out of the methods section of a paper you
already trust and search that. Better still, papers print their accession in a
data availability statement, so read the paper and go straight to it.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The series lists samples but there is no processed data file"}
Some submitters deposit raw reads and nothing else. That's a GEO record
pointing at SRA, and nobody has done the counting. Cross it off,
write down why, and keep the note. The reason is worth as much to you as the
dataset would have been.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The download is one file per sample instead of one table"}
This is common and it isn't wrong. Twelve samples means twelve files you have to
read and join on gene identifier, which is a pandas job from Chapter 20 and
probably an extra evening. Count that cost before you commit to the dataset.
:::

::: {.errfix err="The file you want is labeled controlled access"}
You've hit the tier boundary described above. The request goes through dbGaP
and needs an institutional signing official to sign it. Filter your search to
open-access data at the start, so you stop finding files you can't open.
:::
:::

::: {.checkpoint}
- Name what GEO holds and what SRA holds, and say which one your own question
  needs
- State the group structure of a dataset from its record alone, written as
  groups by samples per group
- Name one thing the metadata doesn't record, for a dataset you chose yourself
- Read a batch variable out of a file name and say what it's confounded with
- Say what sits in TCGA's open tier and why the controlled tier stays shut to
  you
- Write a download size in bytes beside an accession before you fetch it
:::
